title: Why Order Matters in a Gut

scenes.visual: Title card 'Why Order Matters in a Gut' over a cartoon rabbit sitting beside a small pile of soft round pellets. COLOUR MAP (both films, figures, text): food still large GREY blocks; water BLUE; microbes and fermenting chambers GREEN; acid and gastric juice GOLD; blood capillaries RED; lacteal and lymph PALE YELLOW. The gut is always a horizontal tube running left to right, mouth to anus, with the absorbing stretch (small intestine) shaded. Every number appears only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: A rabbit eats some of its own droppings. Why would an animal do that? The answer lies in the shape of the gut itself.
scenes.visual: Cartoon rabbit turns and nibbles a soft pellet; a large question mark pulses above it. The rabbit fades to a faint outline, and a plain horizontal tube draws itself through the outline from mouth (left) to anus (right).
scenes.narration: A rabbit eats some of its own droppings. Why would an animal do that? The answer lies in the shape of the gut itself.

scenes.tts: Many animals, from earthworms to us, have a complete gut. It is a tube, with a mouth at one end and an anus at the other. Food moves one way along it.
scenes.visual: The tube straightens to full screen width, labelled 'mouth' at left and 'anus' at right. A single arrow slides along the tube left to right, label 'one way'. A GREY block enters at the mouth and drifts right.
scenes.narration: Many animals, from earthworms to us, have a complete gut. It is a tube, with a mouth at one end and an anus at the other. Food moves one way along it.

scenes.tts: So each stretch can do its own job, in order. The mouth and stomach break food up. At the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine, bile and pancreatic juice pour in.
scenes.visual: Station labels appear along the tube in order: 'mouth', 'stomach', then one long bracketed stretch 'small intestine' whose first part is labelled 'duodenum', then 'colon'. The GREY block is chopped into smaller GREY blocks at the mouth, churned in the stomach (GOLD acid droplets swirl), then two side pipes join at the duodenum labelled 'bile' and 'pancreatic juice', adding BLUE fluid; the blocks start to shrink there and keep shrinking along the small intestine.
scenes.narration: So each stretch can do its own job, in order. The mouth and stomach break food up. At the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine, bile and pancreatic juice pour in.

scenes.tts: Digestion goes on along the small intestine, the main absorbing stretch. Enzymes there do most of the digesting. Transporters in the wall carry the small pieces across.
scenes.visual: The small-intestine stretch is shaded and long. Along it, GREY blocks keep breaking into grains while grains are already crossing: digestion and absorption overlap. Little gate icons in the wall labelled 'transporters' open for the small grains; a still-large GREY block passes on, breaking down as it goes.
scenes.narration: Digestion goes on along the small intestine, the main absorbing stretch. Enzymes there do most of the digesting. Transporters in the wall carry the small pieces across.

scenes.tts: Simple sugars and amino acids cross into blood capillaries. Most fat is packed into tiny particles that enter the lacteal, a small lymph vessel.
scenes.visual: Zoom into one finger-shaped villus. Grains labelled 'simple sugars' and 'amino acids' slide into a RED capillary loop; grains labelled 'fat' enter a cell, bundle into small particles labelled 'chylomicrons', and leave into a central PALE YELLOW vessel labelled 'lacteal'.
scenes.narration: Simple sugars and amino acids cross into blood capillaries. Most fat is packed into tiny particles that enter the lacteal, a small lymph vessel.

scenes.tts: That is the first half of a rule. Large food molecules must be broken down before or within the stretch that can absorb them.
scenes.visual: Zoom back out to the whole tube. On screen: 'broken down before or within the stretch that can absorb them'. A bracket spans mouth to the end of the small intestine labelled 'break down', overlapping a bracket on the shaded small intestine labelled 'absorb'.
scenes.narration: That is the first half of a rule. Large food molecules must be broken down before or within the stretch that can absorb them.

scenes.tts: Here is the second half. Whatever a stretch does not absorb moves on. Watch the water. The small intestine takes up most of it.
scenes.visual: A thick BLUE bar runs along the tube; side pipes at the mouth, stomach and duodenum thicken it (the gut's own juices). As it passes the shaded small intestine it thins sharply. On screen: 'water leaving = came in + added − absorbed'. No numbers on the bar.
scenes.narration: Here is the second half. Whatever a stretch does not absorb moves on. Watch the water. The small intestine takes up most of it.

scenes.tts: The colon takes up most of what remains. Only a small leftover reaches the end, and it leaves in the feces.
scenes.visual: The BLUE bar thins again across the colon to a thin thread that exits at the anus; the thread is labelled 'small leftover'. Schematic widths, not to scale.
scenes.narration: The colon takes up most of what remains. Only a small leftover reaches the end, and it leaves in the feces.

scenes.tts: Now feed the tube grass. Its main fiber, cellulose, has bonds no vertebrate is known to break with enzymes of its own. Microbes do it, by fermenting the fiber without oxygen.
scenes.visual: GREY blades of grass enter the mouth and pass the small intestine unbroken (labelled 'cellulose'). A GREEN vat appears on the tube, filled with small GREEN microbe cartoons that chew the blades.
scenes.narration: Now feed the tube grass. Its main fiber, cellulose, has bonds no vertebrate is known to break with enzymes of its own. Microbes do it, by fermenting the fiber without oxygen.

scenes.tts: Fermentation makes short-chain fatty acids. The fermenting chamber's own wall absorbs them on the spot, wherever that chamber sits.
scenes.visual: Tiny dots labelled 'short-chain fatty acids' pop out of the GREEN microbes and cross the GREEN vat wall straight into RED capillaries, label 'absorbed where made'.
scenes.narration: Fermentation makes short-chain fatty acids. The fermenting chamber's own wall absorbs them on the spot, wherever that chamber sits.

scenes.tts: But the microbes themselves are food, rich in protein. The acid stomach starts digesting protein. The small intestine finishes the job, and absorbs the amino acids.
scenes.visual: The GREEN microbes glow, tag 'protein'. The GOLD acid stomach lights up, label 'starts protein digestion'; then the shaded small intestine lights up, label 'finishes it, absorbs amino acids'.
scenes.narration: But the microbes themselves are food, rich in protein. The acid stomach starts digesting protein. The small intestine finishes the job, and absorbs the amino acids.

scenes.tts: A cow ferments in front of its acid stomach. Its microbes wash onward, into the acid and then the small intestine. There they are digested.
scenes.visual: Caption 'cow'. The GREEN vat slides to sit before the GOLD stomach compartment. GREEN microbes flow right into the GOLD acid, break into small grains, and the grains cross the shaded small intestine into RED capillaries.
scenes.narration: A cow ferments in front of its acid stomach. Its microbes wash onward, into the acid and then the small intestine. There they are digested.

scenes.tts: A horse ferments in its cecum and colon, after the small intestine. Its microbes are full of protein, and its small intestine is already behind them. Where does that protein go?
scenes.visual: Caption 'horse'. The GREEN vat slides past the shaded small intestine and settles at the cecum and colon. GREEN microbes multiply there; a question card appears over them.
scenes.narration: A horse ferments in its cecum and colon, after the small intestine. Its microbes are full of protein, and its small intestine is already behind them. Where does that protein go?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. The question card holds over the horse's GREEN hindgut vat; 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: Most of it leaves in the droppings. The stretch that absorbs amino acids is already behind it.
scenes.visual: Most GREEN microbes flow out at the anus, label 'most microbial protein lost'. A few dots still cross the vat wall (the fatty acids, still absorbed on the spot).
scenes.narration: Most of it leaves in the droppings. The stretch that absorbs amino acids is already behind it.

scenes.tts: A rabbit ferments mainly in its cecum, after the small intestine too. So it makes soft pellets from its cecum, and eats them. The microbes go round again, through the stomach and small intestine.
scenes.visual: Caption 'rabbit'. Soft GREEN pellets form in the cecum, exit, and a curved arrow carries them back to the mouth. They pass the GOLD stomach and the shaded small intestine, where they break into grains that cross into RED capillaries.
scenes.narration: A rabbit ferments mainly in its cecum, after the small intestine too. So it makes soft pellets from its cecum, and eats them. The microbes go round again, through the stomach and small intestine.

scenes.tts: That is why a rabbit eats some of its droppings. Food must be broken down before or within the stretch that can absorb it.
scenes.visual: Recap strip: cow (vat before the stomach, microbes digested), horse (vat after, protein lost), rabbit (vat after, pellets loop back). The rabbit from the opening nibbles a pellet; the question mark becomes a tick.
scenes.narration: That is why a rabbit eats some of its droppings. Food must be broken down before or within the stretch that can absorb it.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex. LINE: 'Break food down before or within the stretch that can absorb it.'
